                                          PROJECT NO. 58481


      RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                          §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION

                                                       §



                                    (STAFF RECOMMENDATION)


                    PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC §25.194


 1   The Public Utility Commission of Texas (commission) proposes new 16 Texas Administrative

 2   Code (TAC) §25.194 relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards. This proposed rule will

 3   implement Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) §37.0561, as enacted by Senate Bill (SB) 6

 4   during the Texas 89th Regular Legislative Session. The new rule will implement new PURA

 5   §37.0561, which requires the commission to establish standards for interconnecting large load

 6   customers in the ERCOT power region in a manner designed to support business development in

 7   this state while minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system

 8   reliability. The new rule will require a large load customer, before the large load customer can be

 9   included in an ERCOT interconnection study, to execute an intermediate agreement that requires

10   the large load customer to provide certain disclosures and post financial security in the amount of

11   $50,000 per megawatt (MW). The new rule will also require a large load customer, not later than

12   3060 days after ERCOT completes the interconnection study, to execute an interconnection

13   agreement that requires the large load customer to update its disclosures, pay a non-refundable

14   interconnection fee maintain financial security in the amount of $50,000 per MW; post financial

15   security creditable toward the customer’s obligations for significant equipment or services and

16   contribution in aid of construction; pay contribution in aid of construction for direct
      Project No. 58481        (Staff Recommendation) Proposal for Publication                 Page 2 of 42


 1   interconnection costs; and post financial security for system upgrades., which is independent of

 2   and not creditable against the interconnection security. Additionally, the new rule will set forth

 3   the consequences of withdrawing all or a portion of requested peak demand or contracted peak

 4   demand and the consequences of failing to satisfy a milestone in the large load customer’s schedule

 5   for phased energization. Finally, the new rule will set forth the terms for refundrelease of financial

 6   security for a large load customer that energizes. The new rule will also establish transitional

 7   provisions through applicability designations, integrated within the intermediate agreement and

 8   interconnection agreement requirements, for a large load customer that has executed an

 9   interconnection agreement or an intermediate agreement before the effective date of this section.

10

11   Growth Impact Statement

12   The agency provides the following governmental growth impact statement for the proposed rule,

13   as required by Texas Government Code §2001.0221. The agency has determined that for each

14   year of the first five years that the proposed rule is in effect, the following statements will apply:

15   (1) the proposed rule will not create a government program and will not eliminate a government

16   program;

17   (2) implementation of the proposed rule will not require the creation of new employee positions

18   and will not require the elimination of existing employee positions;

19   (3) implementation of the proposed rule will not require an increase and will not require a decrease

20   in future legislative appropriations to the agency;

21   (4) the proposed rule will not require an increase and will not require a decrease in fees paid to the

22   agency;

 3   (7) the proposed rule will not change the number of individuals subject to the rule's applicability;

 4   and

 5   (8) the proposed rule will not affect this state’s economy.

 6

 7   Fiscal Impact on Small and Micro-Businesses and Rural Communities

 8   There is no adverse economic effect anticipated for small businesses, micro-businesses, or rural

 9   communities as a result of implementing the proposed rule. Accordingly, no economic impact

10   statement or regulatory flexibility analysis is required under Texas Government Code

11   §2006.002(c).

12

13   Takings Impact Analysis

14   The commission has determined that the proposed rule will not be a taking of private property as

15   defined in chapter 2007 of the Texas Government Code.

16

17   Fiscal Impact on State and Local Government

18   Jessie Horn, Sr. Counsel, Rules and Projects Division, has determined that for the first five-year

19   period the proposed rule is in effect, there will be no fiscal implications for the state or for units of

20   local government under Texas Government Code §2001.024(a)(4) as a result of enforcing or

21   administering the sections.

 1   Public Benefits

 2   Ms. Horn has determined that for each year of the first five years the proposed section is in effect

 3   the public benefit anticipated as a result of enforcing the section will be increased transparency

 4   and support of business development. There will be a probable economic cost to persons required

 5   to comply with the rule under Texas Government Code §2001.024(a)(5) because PURA §37.0561,

 6   which the rule implements, requires large load customers to make financial commitments.

 7

 8   Local Employment Impact Statement

 9   For each year of the first five years the proposed section is in effect, there should be no effect on

10   a local economy; therefore, no local employment impact statement is required under Texas

11   Government Code §2001.022.

12

13   Costs to Regulated Persons

14   Texas Government Code §2001.0045(b) does not apply to this rulemaking because the commission

15   is expressly excluded under subsection §2001.0045(c)(7).

16

17   Public Hearing

18   Commission staff will conduct a public hearing on this rulemaking if requested in accordance with

19   Texas Government Code §2001.029. The request for a public hearing must be received by April

20   17, 2026. If a request for public hearing is received, commission staff will file in this project a

21   notice of hearing.

 2   Interested persons may file comments electronically through the interchange on the commission’s

 3   website or by submitting a paper copy to Central Records, Public Utility Commission of Texas,

 4   1701 North Congress Avenue, P.O. Box 13326, Austin, Texas 78711-3326. Initial comments must

 5   be filed by April 17, 2026. Comments should be organized in a manner consistent with the

 1   §25.194. Large Load Interconnection Standards.

 2   (a)    Purpose and Scope. This section sets forth the standards and criteria for an electric utility,

 3          a municipally owned utility, and electric cooperative to interconnect a large load customer

 4          to the ERCOT system. Nothing in this section limits the authority of a municipally owned

 5          utility or an electric cooperative to impose electric service requirements for large load

 6          customers on their systems in addition to the standards adopted under this section.

 7

 8   (b)    Applicability. This section applies to a large load customer that seeks:

 9          (1)    a new interconnection that is equal to or exceeds 75 megawatts (MW);

10          (2)    an expanded interconnection that equals or exceeds 75 MW for the first time; and

11          (3)    an expanded interconnection that exceeds 75 MW by 75 MW or more.

PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC §25.194
The Public Utility Commission of Texas (commission) proposes new 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) §25.194 relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards.  This proposed rule will implement Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) §37.0561, as enacted by Senate Bill (SB) 6 during the Texas 89th Regular Legislative Session.  The new rule will implement new PURA §37.0561, which requires the commission to establish standards for interconnecting large load customers in the ERCOT power region in a manner designed to support business development in this state while minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability.  The new rule will require a large load customer, before the large load customer can be included in an ERCOT interconnection study, to execute an intermediate agreement that requires the large load customer to provide certain disclosures and post financial security in the amount of $50,000 per megawatt (MW).  The new rule will also require a large load customer, not later than  days after ERCOT completes the interconnection study, to execute an interconnection agreement that requires the large load customer to update its disclosures, in the amount of $50,000 per MWfor significant equipment or services; pay contribution in aid of construction for direct interconnection costs; and post financial security for system upgrades  Additionally, the new rule will set forth the consequences of withdrawing all or a portion of requested peak demand or contracted peak demand and the consequences of failing to satisfy a milestone in the large load customer’s schedule for phased energization.  Finally, the new rule will set forth the terms for  of financial security for a large load customer that energizes.

(a)	Purpose and Scope.  This section sets forth the standards and criteria for an electric utility, a municipally owned utility, and electric cooperative to interconnect a large load customer to the ERCOT system.  Nothing in this section limits the authority of a municipally owned utility or an electric cooperative to impose electric service requirements for large load customers on their systems in addition to the standards adopted under this section.

(b)	Applicability.  This section applies to a large load customer that seeks:
(1)	a new interconnection that is equal to or exceeds 75 megawatts (MW); 
(2)	an expanded interconnection that equals or exceeds 75 MW for the first time; and 
(3)	an expanded interconnection that exceeds 75 MW by 75 MW or more.

(1)	Backup generating facilities -- Generation facilities or energy storage facilities that are not capable of operating, or are not configured to operate, in parallel with the ERCOT system and cannot export energy to the ERCOT system. 
(2)	Competitively sensitive information -- Competitively sensitive information includes exact site locations, such as parcel identifiers or property boundaries; commercial terms, such as pricing or internal development prioritization; proprietary architectural, operational, or compute-deployment strategies; and financing structures.  Competitively sensitive information does not include the identity of a large load customer; general site location, such as load zone; requested or contracted peak demand; timing of energization; or whether an interconnection request is associated with the same applicant or affiliated entities. 
(3)	Contracted peak demand -- The total non-coincident peak demand that a large load customer requests that an interconnecting DSP or an interconnecting TSP serve at a site as stated interconnection agreement.

(5)	Interconnecting transmission service provider (TSP) -- The electric utility, municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative that owns and operates the facilities necessary to interconnect the large load customer to the ERCOT system.

        Schaper Energy Consulting LLC (“Respondent”) advises large load customers in the ERCOT

State of Texas. Respondent provides these comments to assist Commission Staff in their ongoing efforts

to refine large load interconnection standard language.


                           II.​   DRAFT PFP MODIFICATION SUMMARY


        Respondent offers for the Commission’s consideration the following clarifications to the Proposal

For Publication dated March 16, 2026. We have provided both comprehensive redline edits (attached as

Appendix A) and an accompanying Word file markup for ease of review. Senate Bill 6 directs the

Commission to establish interconnection standards that support business development in this state while

minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability.          The

modifications summarized below are organized according to how each category of proposed changes

advances one or more of those statutory objectives.


I. Financial Security Architecture


        The most significant structural change in the redline is the reorganization of the rule’s financial

security framework from a non-refundable fee model to a creditable, maintained-security model. Staff’s

draft imposed a $50,000/MW non-refundable interconnection fee at the interconnection agreement stage,
 separate financial security for significant equipment and services, separate CIAC, and separate financial

security for system upgrades.     That structure, while well-intentioned, creates overlapping financial

obligations that could require a large load customer to have multiple layers of security outstanding

simultaneously for related costs, discouraging the very business development SB 6 seeks to promote. The

redline consolidates these obligations into a coherent, single-pot crediting architecture in which each

dollar posted by the customer is applied against the customer’s aggregate financial threshold, while

preserving the ratepayer protections that SB 6 requires through independent, purpose-built security for

system upgrades.


The financial security framework operates across three categories:


        Intermediate agreement security. New language in subsection (d)(10) repositions the

$50,000/MW financial security requirement at the intermediate agreement stage as “intermediate

agreement security,” a formally defined term in subsection (c)(9) that functions as a maintained security

pool through which current billable obligations may be satisfied during the intermediate agreement stage.

The revised structure establishes a single-pot, transferable crediting mechanism under which amounts

paid for significant equipment, services, and CIAC are credited against the intermediate agreement

security obligation on a dollar-for-dollar basis, with the remaining intermediate agreement security

required to be maintained, supplemented as necessary, and carried forward into the interconnection

agreement stage. If the large load customer withdraws before executing an interconnection agreement,

the balance of the intermediate agreement security is released after application to any outstanding

amounts owed, providing the utility with cost recovery while returning unneeded security to the customer.

This approach supports business development by ensuring that committed capital is not unnecessarily tied

up in redundant security instruments, while still protecting ratepayers and utilities against the costs of

withdrawal.
         Interconnection security (formerly non-refundable interconnection fee). We acknowledge

Staff’s objective in treating the interconnection fee as non-refundable, namely, to protect ratepayers from

stranded infrastructure costs if a load customer withdraws.          We share that objective.      However,

repositioning the interconnection fee as a maintained, creditable financial security construct is both less

disruptive to in-flight and future projects and more consistent with cost-causation principles, while still

ensuring that load customers stand behind their commitments without imposing unnecessary forfeiture.

As revised, the interconnection security in subsection (f)(7) requires $50,000/MW of contracted peak

demand, with the intermediate agreement security credited toward that requirement. Amounts paid for

significant equipment or services and CIAC are also credited on a dollar-for-dollar basis. Self-contained

release provisions in subsection (f)(7)(E) govern the disposition of remaining balances upon withdrawal,

milestone failure, or energization, ensuring that ratepayer exposure is addressed at the point where the risk

actually resides rather than through a blanket non-refundable charge that would penalize committed load

customers regardless of whether their interconnection actually requires material upgrades.


        System upgrade security. Financial security for system upgrades is compartmentalized as an

independent obligation, separate from the intermediate agreement security and the interconnection

security, to reflect the reality that not all large load customers trigger system upgrades. Interconnection

studies routinely identify sites where existing transmission capacity is sufficient to serve the requested

load without network reinforcement. Load customers who select project sites where no system upgrades

are required should not be burdened with security obligations sized to address upgrade costs that their

interconnection does not impose; recognizing this distinction directly supports business development by

rewarding customers who site projects to minimize grid impact. The obligation to post system upgrade

security is accordingly deferred until the interconnection study is complete and the costs of required

upgrades, if any, have been determined and allocated to the specific large load customer whose load

necessitates those upgrades. Where no upgrades are required, no system upgrade security is owed. A

new self-contained release and forfeiture framework in subsection (f)(10)(E) provides for full forfeiture to
 the TSP’s rate base upon post-interconnection-agreement withdrawal or a 12-month milestone failure,

20%-per-year release upon energization beginning one year after the in-service date, and full release not

later than five years after the in-service date. This forfeiture-to-rate-base mechanism directly addresses

the stranded-cost risk that SB 6 targets, ensuring that if a customer walks away from a project that

required system upgrades, those costs are recovered through the interconnecting TSP’s rate base rather

than socialized to other ratepayers.


II. Cost Recovery and Billing Flexibility


        Significant equipment and services. We believe it is appropriate to expand the scope of

financial security for significant equipment and services beyond Staff’s narrow trigger of equipment with

a lead time of at least six months. In practice, the costs necessary to interconnect a large load customer

encompass a range of equipment and services that may not individually meet a six-month threshold but

collectively represent substantial utility expenditure undertaken in reliance on the customer’s

commitment. The redline replaces the lead-time trigger with a broader “full anticipated costs” standard

covering all estimated equipment and services required to interconnect the large load customer, with

added billing flexibility (up-front or as-incurred at utility option), 60-day true-up requirements against

actual costs, and provisions for advanced procurement agreements during the intermediate agreement

stage. Expanding coverage to the full anticipated cost of interconnection ensures that utilities are never

required to procure equipment or services on an unsecured basis, which minimizes the potential for

stranded costs. At the same time, billing flexibility and true-up provisions give both the utility and the

large load customer practical tools to manage cash flow and cost uncertainty without sacrificing financial

discipline.


        Contribution in aid of construction (CIAC). CIAC non-refundability is fully preserved.

However, the requirement for a single up-front cash payment at interconnection agreement execution is

replaced with the flexibility to either post security for the full anticipated CIAC amount and pay as costs
 are incurred, or prepay in cash. This allows utilities to collect overarching security and bill direct

interconnection costs to the large load customer as they are actually incurred, rather than requiring the full

amount at signing. A structured 60-day reconciliation process ensures amounts collected are trued up

against actual costs, with any overpayment refunded and any underpayment invoiced, while CIAC itself

remains non-refundable. These modifications ensure that all direct interconnection costs continue to be

borne entirely by the large load customer, as SB 6 intends, while giving developers the practical billing

flexibility needed to bring large-scale projects to fruition in Texas.


III. Site Control and Qualifying Property Interests.


        The site control provisions in subsections (d)(1) and (f)(1) are revised to align with the direction

of Staff’s latest draft while providing more comprehensive coverage of acceptable property interests.

Staff’s PFP draft identified three qualifying forms of site control (a lease, a deed, or a purchase and sale

agreement) but did not address purchase options, interests held through affiliates or trustees, or leasehold

options, each of which is commonly used in large-scale infrastructure development. The redline replaces

these provisions with a standard four-prong property interest test (fee simple ownership, leasehold,

written option to purchase or lease, or executed purchase contract) and permits the large load customer to

demonstrate site control through an affiliated company, through a trustee, or directly in its name. This

framework is consistent with the site control requirements established in ERCOT’s existing generator

interconnection rules and is reflective of the range of property interests that serious, committed load

customers typically hold at the time an interconnection request is submitted.            By broadening the

recognized forms of qualifying site control to encompass standard commercial development structures,

these revisions support business development without in any way diminishing the commitment that a

demonstrated property interest represents.


IV. Transitional and Applicability Provisions.
           Transitional and applicability standards are necessary to provide clarity to market participants

who have already made substantial financial commitments in reliance on the existing interconnection

framework. Projects that are currently in-flight under existing interconnection agreements, or that are

proceeding under preliminary agreements with their interconnecting utilities, represent billions of dollars

of committed private capital and tens of thousands of anticipated construction and operations jobs across

the state. Retroactive application of new standards to these projects would undermine the investment

certainty that SB 6 seeks to promote and could cause project delays or cancellations that would directly

harm business development in Texas. The redline incorporates transitional provisions directly into the

operative provisions to which they apply, including study fee reconciliation for in-flight requests in

subsection (d)(9)(F), transition treatment for pre-existing preliminary agreements in subsection (d)(12),

and new subsection (f)(11), which establishes an applicability pathway under which a large load customer

that has, prior to the effective date of the new rule, (i) executed all applicable facilities extension or

interconnection agreements required to fund interconnection facilities, (ii) provided financial security or

made all required payments, and (iii) issued notice to proceed for construction, is deemed to have satisfied

the requirements of the interconnection agreement subsection. Even where system upgrade costs have not

yet been allocated, the redline provides for those costs to be addressed through a post-study amendment,

ensuring that no project is exempt from contributing to the system upgrade costs its load imposes. These

revisions should materially improve market understanding of how the new standards apply to projects

already underway and should help preserve continued investment and hiring during the rulemaking

period.


V. Release, Forfeiture, and Withdrawal Framework


          Withdrawal, non-utilized capacity, and energization. The proposed changes align the

treatment of withdrawal, non-utilized capacity, and energization with SB 6’s core policy objective of

distinguishing between customers that make meaningful, finance-backed commitments to the Texas grid

and those that do not.       As revised, the framework rewards customers that advance projects with
 substantial posted financial security, thereby protecting ratepayers against the risk of stranded or

underfunded system upgrade costs, while preserving a clear penalty for customers that withdraw after

making such commitments by directing forfeited amounts into rate base to offset system upgrades that

would otherwise be left underfunded. The prior 80/20 forfeiture-to-rate-base construct is eliminated.

Subsections (g) (withdrawal), (h) (non-utilized capacity), and (i) (energization) are reorganized into

streamlined procedural provisions governing notice, drawdown, and ERCOT reallocation that

cross-reference the operative release and forfeiture mechanics in subsections (f)(7)(E) and (f)(10)(E). The

term “refund” is replaced throughout with “release” when referring to financial security, to reflect the

legal distinction between returning a fee and releasing a security instrument. The non-utilized capacity

trigger is extended from six months to twelve months to provide large load customers with a

commercially reasonable runway to meet energization milestones, consistent with the realities of

large-scale infrastructure construction. A shorter trigger would risk penalizing committed customers for

construction delays outside their control, which would discourage business development in Texas without

providing meaningful additional ratepayer protection.


                                            III.​   CLOSING


        We believe these modifications, while comprehensive, offer Staff a workable framework that

honors existing interconnection commitments, provides market participants with clarity on the scope and

sequencing of financial obligations, prevents stranded infrastructure costs, ensures that all direct

interconnection costs are borne by the large load customer, and addresses system upgrade risk through

independent, purpose-built security backed by the full allocated cost of required upgrades.
